paragraphs.source_en: From the fifteenth to the seventeenth centuries, most rulers dabbled in alchemy and magic. Even Philip II’s Escorial housed several laboratories where the king supervised the distillation of essences and experiments in the transmutation of metals. Alchemy and the occult were not seen, however, as diversions from rulership. They were central to it, for the realms of magic and of hidden truth were thought to hold the solution to how the world might be brought into conformity with the cosmic order. They also inspired other activities of kingship, from the way royal collections were organized to the commissioning of works of art. Occult knowledge was a self-enclosed intellectual system, which was tantalizingly opaque and yet logically built up, albeit from dubious first principles.
